At least five people dead in Miami plane crash: Officials

An Amazon cargo plane crashed at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon after overrunning the runway, according to multiple accounts. The Boeing 767-300, operated by 21 Air, was flying from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and came to rest in a field adjacent to the airport. At least five people were confirmed dead, with five others injured. Firefighters responded to a scene engulfed in flames and smoke, conducting search and rescue operations. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) confirmed the crash and stated it would investigate. Miami-Dade County officials, including Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz and Mayor Daniella Levine Cava, expressed condolences and thanked first responders for their quick action.

The crash led to a ground stop at Miami International Airport, halting all flights for several hours. Fire crews worked to contain a fuel leak and extinguish the fire, with some victims trapped in vehicles struck by the plane. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and the FAA are both involved in the investigation. Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel confirmed the incident and expressed condolences to the families of the victims.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Guardian both report that the plane struck several vehicles, but The Guardian specifies that the plane crashed into multiple vehicles and trapped several people inside them. The Daily Caller and FOX News also mention that the plane struck multiple vehicles, but FOX News adds that some victims required "extrication" by technical rescue personnel. The Guardian and Al Jazeera note that three victims were in critical condition, while The Daily Caller and FOX News state that three were taken to a trauma center in critical condition. The Washington Examiner and The Guardian report that the plane came to rest in a field adjacent to the airport, while FOX News and Al Jazeera mention that the plane was disabled at the northwest end of the airport. The Guardian and Al Jazeera mention that the cause of the crash is under investigation, while The Washington Examiner and The Daily Caller do not specify the cause.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Guardian · The Daily Caller · FOX News · NPR · Al Jazeera

Trump envoys and Putin discussed ‘next steps’ for ending Ukraine war, White House says

U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday to discuss "substantive plans for next steps" toward ending the war in Ukraine, according to a White House official. The meeting lasted about three hours, and the envoys are set to visit Kyiv on Sunday for further talks. The White House stated that the plans would be announced in "coming weeks." Russian President Putin expressed confidence in Russia's battlefield progress and emphasized the need to address "all the root causes of the conflict." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that Russian attacks on Kyiv and Boryspil international airports were a reaction to the U.S. envoys' visit and warned that Ukraine would adjust its operations in Russian airspace. Both sides agreed to a short pause in airstrikes on each other’s capitals during the envoys' visit.

The meeting in Moscow was part of a renewed push for peace amid escalating aerial attacks by both sides. The U.S. has been trying to revive stalled peace talks, but progress has been slow as U.S. attention has shifted to its war with Iran. The envoys were joined by officials from the National Security Council, State Department, and Treasury Department during the discussions. Putin thanked the U.S. for releasing former Marine Robert Gilman from Russian custody and acknowledged the pause in airstrikes. Zelenskyy said Ukraine would not target Moscow with drones and missiles during the envoys' visit and urged Russia to reciprocate.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and BBC report that Zelenskyy linked Russian attacks on Kyiv and Boryspil airports to the U.S. envoys' visit, while the BBC adds that Zelenskyy described the Donbas region as "difficult" and insisted Ukraine would not give up territory there. The Guardian and Axios note that Putin told the envoys Russia was making "real progress" on the battlefield, while the BBC states Ukrainian officials claim Russia suffered 42,000 casualties in August. The Associated Press and Axios mention that the U.S. envoys were joined by Gene Lange, the acting sanctions czar, during the Moscow meeting, which the other accounts do not mention. The Guardian and NPR report that the envoys are visiting Kyiv for the first time in their roles, while the BBC notes that they had never visited Kyiv before.

Sources The Guardian · NPR · ABC News · Axios · Associated Press · BBC

Far-right AfD wins key German state election but falls just short of majority

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a significant victory in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, securing 43.8% of the vote and 39 seats in an 83-member parliament. The party fell three seats short of an absolute majority needed to govern alone. The Christian Democratic Union (CDU), led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, saw its support drop to 17.2%, winning 15 seats. The Social Democrats (SPD), Greens, and the Left party each won around 9% to 8.6% of the vote, securing eight seats apiece. The BSW party, which opposes the "firewall" against AfD, won 5.3% and five seats. Turnout reached a record high of 76.5% in the Guardian, while CBS News reported 77.8%.

AfD candidate Ulrich Siegmund claimed the result was a mandate to govern and called for a "self-confident signal" for Germany. He attributed the party's success to Merz's campaign efforts. Alice Weidel, AfD’s co-leader, said the result gave the party a "clear government mandate." The CDU described its result as "bitter" and ruled out any coalition with AfD. Siegmund also outlined the party's "remigration" policy, which includes deportations and segregation of refugees.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and CBS News differ on turnout, with the Guardian reporting 76.5% and CBS News 77.8%. The Guardian mentions that the CDU described its result as "bitter" and ruled out any discussion over Merz’s future, while CBS News does not include this detail. The Axios account notes that AfD won 44% in Saxony-Anhalt, while the Guardian and CBS News report 43.8%. The Newsweek account includes specific voter transfer analysis and mentions that 170,000 AfD votes came from previous nonvoters, which the other accounts do not include.

Sources The Guardian · Al Jazeera · NPR · CBS News · Axios · Newsweek

Armed assailant lunged at Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, campaign says

An armed individual lunged at Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, during a campaign stop at the Canfield Fair on Sunday, according to multiple outlets. Campaign officials confirmed that several people were injured in the incident, though Acton herself was not harmed. The suspect, identified as Patrick Havas, 38, was arrested and is expected to face charges of assault and disorderly conduct. Mahoning County Sheriff Jerry Greene described Havas as having knocked down two older adults during the incident. The Ohio State Highway Patrol was involved in the arrest, and Havas was found to be carrying two handguns and a set of brass knuckles. Campaign officials and political figures, including Acton’s opponent Vivek Ramaswamy, condemned the attack as unacceptable and called for an end to political violence.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and Al Jazeera both mention that Havas knocked down two older adults, but only Al Jazeera specifies that the sheriff told 21 News about this. CBS News and Washington Examiner also note that Havas knocked over two older adults, with CBS adding that one of them fell to the ground. Newsweek and Just The News do not mention the specific detail about the older adults being knocked down. Additionally, Newsweek is the only outlet that identifies Havas as a registered Republican and licensed nurse, based on records reviewed by the publication. The Guardian and Al Jazeera both mention that Ramaswamy condemned the attack, but only the Guardian includes a quote from his communications director, Connie Luck, stating the incident was “completely unacceptable.” The Guardian also includes a quote from Abdul El-Sayad, a Michigan Democratic Senate candidate, denouncing the attack, which is absent from the other accounts.

Sources The Guardian · Al Jazeera · CBS News · Washington Examiner · Newsweek · Just The News

Lindsay Clancy murder trial ends in dramatic deadlock – what comes next?

Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial ended in a mistrial after jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict. The jury deadlocked 11 to 1, with one juror refusing to convict despite expressing reasonable doubt. Clancy, a 36-year-old former nurse, did not deny killing her three children but pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, citing postpartum psychosis and overmedication. Prosecutors argued she was fully aware of her actions. The mistrial followed a motion by Clancy’s defense to replace the holdout juror, which the court denied. Clancy remains in a hospital, and a new trial date is pending. The case has drawn national attention, with supporters and critics divided over her mental health and legal culpability.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and Straight Arrow News both report that Clancy strangled her children, while Straight Arrow News adds that she jumped from a second-story window. The Guardian and Slate describe the jury deadlock as 11 to 1, while Straight Arrow News does not specify the vote count. The Guardian and FOX News both mention the holdout juror’s refusal to apply the legal standard, but FOX News adds that the holdout was a man, while The Guardian does not specify the juror’s gender. The Guardian and Slate describe the holdout juror as expressing reasonable doubt, while FOX News adds that the juror refused to apply the legal standard. The Guardian and Slate mention the complexity of Massachusetts law on criminal responsibility, while Straight Arrow News does not address this. The Guardian and Slate describe the public reaction to the mistrial, while Straight Arrow News focuses on a separate case in Illinois.

Sources The Guardian · Slate · FOX News · The Daily Wire · Washington Examiner · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

Trump administration makes another Supreme Court appeal on mail ballot fight

The Trump administration has filed a third appeal with the Supreme Court seeking to enforce new restrictions on mail ballots ahead of the midterms. The filing follows a federal judge’s order blocking the implementation of the rules, which were based on an executive order from President Trump. The administration argues that the current injunction creates confusion and chaos as states begin mailing ballots, with some states already having started the process. Solicitor General John Sauer stated that once ballots enter the mailstream, they cannot be retrieved, and the voluntary nature of compliance under the injunction risks undermining election integrity.

The dispute centers on Trump’s executive order directing the Postal Service to implement new rules for mail ballots, including unique barcodes and specific envelope requirements. The administration claims these measures are lawful and aimed at improving mail handling and preventing fraud. However, Democratic states and voting rights groups argue the changes are unconstitutional, while election officials say there is insufficient time to adjust their systems to meet the new federal directives. The Supreme Court has previously allowed the plan to proceed but has not ruled on its legality.

The outcome of the legal battle could significantly impact the November elections, where control of Congress is at stake. Nearly one-third of U.S. voters cast ballots by mail, making the issue critical for both parties. The administration continues to push for a stay of the injunction, arguing that it is necessary to ensure compliance with the new rules and maintain election security.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News and The Guardian both state that the Supreme Court has allowed the plan to move forward but not ruled on its legality. FOX News and Straight Arrow News also mention this, but FOX News adds that the administration disputes the claim that the rule dictates ballot content, determines voter eligibility, or governs how ballots are counted. The New York Post does not mention this specific point, instead focusing on the administration’s framing of the restrictions as "commonsense changes."

Sources CBS News · Washington Examiner · The Guardian · Straight Arrow News · FOX News · New York Post

Trump Posts Map Renaming New Mexico as 'New America'

President Donald Trump shared a map on Truth Social Sunday showing New Mexico with the word "Mexico" crossed out and replaced with "America," suggesting the state could be renamed "New America." The post came days after Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America" amid trade tensions with Canada. The White House did not immediately confirm any formal plan for renaming New Mexico, though the post appeared alongside other unrelated content, including an AI-generated video of Trump kicking over a sign at Lake Ontario.

The idea of renaming New Mexico has circulated before, with fact-checkers debunking similar claims in the past. Trump has previously attempted to rename geographic features, including the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America and reverting Mt. Denali to Mt. McKinley. While some private companies and international bodies have adopted Trump's name changes, states are not subject to federal renaming efforts. New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham criticized the post, stating the state's name is not up for debate and highlighting state efforts to support working families.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and Newsweek both mention that Trump's post was part of a broader series of AI-generated images and memes, including one declaring "The Moon Is Ours." The Washington Examiner and New York Post do not reference the moon post or the AI-generated content. The Daily Wire and Newsweek also note that Trump did not clarify whether the New Mexico post was a joke or a serious proposal, while the Washington Examiner and New York Post do not address this ambiguity. The New York Post and FOX News both mention that renaming a state is not possible through executive action, while the Daily Wire and Newsweek do not explicitly state this.

Sources The Daily Wire · Washington Examiner · FOX News · Newsweek · New York Post

No source labeled lean-left or left covered this story.

Pete Hegseth faces criticism for leadership style and military decisions

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has drawn scrutiny for his leadership approach and military decisions. The Pentagon has faced internal challenges, including the resignation of Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who clashed with Hegseth. Hegseth has also faced criticism for firing or blocking promotions of over 80 generals and admirals, with reports indicating that a significant portion of those removed were Black or female. The military has raised concerns about extended deployments in the Middle East, with some commanders objecting to the plans. Hegseth has also been criticized for his handling of civilian harm mitigation, particularly following strikes in Iran that resulted in civilian casualties. The US has not formally admitted responsibility for the strikes, though an investigation is ongoing.

The resumption of strikes on Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz has raised questions about the US's objectives in the conflict with Iran. These strikes, which included attacks on mainland Iran and Iranian islands in the Gulf, caused multiple casualties, including a six-year-old child in Kuhestak. Iranian authorities have labeled the deaths a war crime, drawing comparisons to previous strikes that killed over 150 people, including children, in Minab. The US has not officially acknowledged responsibility for the Minab strike, which occurred on the first day of the war.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that retired major general Randy Manner called Hegseth a "clear and present danger to the national security of the United States and the world," while The Dispatch and FOX News do not include this specific quote. The Dispatch mentions that Hegseth has fired or blocked promotions of more than 80 generals and admirals, with 60 percent of those removed being Black or female, while The Guardian does not specify the demographic breakdown. FOX News states that the Pentagon has put several conservative influencers on the payroll, a detail not mentioned in The Guardian or The Dispatch.

Sources The Guardian · The Dispatch · FOX News

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

The brief ends here.

Trump-backed group announces $10m ad spend for midterm Senate race in Texas

A political group associated with United States President Donald Trump has announced it will spend $10m on television and digital advertisements in the state of Texas ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. The Saturday filing with the Federal Election Commission (FEC) represents the first major spend in a general election by MAGA, Inc, a super PAC named for Trump’s “Make America Great Again” movement. The advertisements are expected to heavily target Democratic candidate James Talarico, a 37-year-old state representative running for the US Senate against Trump-backed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Speculation abounds that Democrats may have a chance of flipping one of Texas’s Senate seats for the first time since 1993. Paxton has weathered a series of scandals, even facing a state impeachment trial. Still, Democrats have repeatedly faced withering defeats in Texas, having failed to win a statewide office there in more than three decades.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and The Daily Wire both report that MAGA Inc. is spending $10m on ads in Texas, but The Daily Wire adds that Trump has vowed to spend up to $500 million in outside money before Election Day. The Daily Wire also mentions Elon Musk’s America PAC spending over $800,000 on Texas races, which is not included in Al Jazeera. The Washington Examiner focuses on the GOP midterm convention in Dallas, while Just The News includes a detailed list of speakers and attendees, which is absent in Al Jazeera. Axios and The Daily Caller provide different perspectives on the political strategy, with Axios highlighting the GOP’s acceptance of a Trump-focused campaign and The Daily Caller suggesting Republicans may be trying to lose the midterms.

Sources Al Jazeera · Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · Just The News · Axios · The Daily Caller

Russian attacks kill 4 in Ukraine as Moscow and Kyiv prepare for visit by US envoys

Russian attacks killed four people in Ukraine overnight, as Moscow and Kyiv await the arrival of U.S. envoys to begin a new push for peace in the Kremlin’s 4 1/2-year-old invasion. The planned visit by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, is hoped to revive peace talks amid escalating aerial attacks by both sides. The air war between Russia and Ukraine has intensified as troops have struggled to make progress along the 1,250-kilometer (775-mile) front line. Russia has recently been using fast-flying, jet-powered drones, and the recurring wail of air-raid sirens has become part of daily life in Kyiv. The strikes come despite a message from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy Friday saying that Ukraine would halt air attacks during Witkoff and Kushner’s visit and urging Moscow to do the same.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed he will meet the envoys on Sunday after they visit Moscow on Saturday to hold talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Witkoff and Kushner have led U.S. President Donald Trump’s efforts to broker a peace deal, but a gulf remains between the two warring sides. Zelenskyy said Ukraine is ready to observe a ceasefire and have a “substantive conversation” with Witkoff and Kushner. “From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv,” he said.

Where the accounts differ

AP and BBC both report that four people were killed in an attack in the Dnipropetrovsk region, while Straight Arrow News reports five people were killed in the same attack. FOX News and CBS News do not mention the number of casualties in the Dnipropetrovsk attack. AP and BBC attribute the attack to Russian strikes, while Straight Arrow News attributes it to Russian missiles. CBS News reports that Russia ordered a three-day suspension of strikes against Kyiv, while AP and BBC report that Zelenskyy urged Russia to do the same. FOX News states that the meeting with Putin concluded without any breakthroughs, while CBS News and Axios report that the meeting was constructive and substantive. Axios reports that Russia dramatically increased its drone and missile attacks on Ukraine, while the other accounts do not mention this escalation.

Sources Associated Press · Axios · BBC · Straight Arrow News · FOX News · CBS News

Iran claims strike on US ship in Strait of Hormuz as fighting escalates

The U.S. military struck three Iranian oil tankers in response to missile attacks on two U.S. warships, according to CENTCOM. Iran claimed it struck an unmanned U.S. vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, escalating tensions. The conflict, which began in February, has seen intermittent fighting since a ceasefire agreement collapsed in June. The latest strikes come after a week of relative calm, with both sides targeting each other's assets in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters.

The U.S. and Iran have been engaged in a cycle of retaliation, with the U.S. targeting Iranian oil tankers and Iran responding with attacks on U.S. vessels. The strikes have disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global oil. Iran has threatened to increase its attacks if the U.S. continues to block its ports and target its ships. The U.S. has also imposed sanctions on financial institutions linked to Iran's shadow network, aiming to cut off its access to international markets.

Where the accounts differ

AP reports that Iran claimed it struck an unmanned U.S. vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, while CBS News states that Iran said it attacked a U.S. naval drone attempting to enter the strait. NPR and Axios both mention that the U.S. struck three Iranian oil tankers, but NPR adds that one of the tankers was in the Gulf of Oman and that its crew was forced to abandon ship. BBC notes that Iranian state media confirmed the U.S. strikes and reported that the crews of the attacked tankers were taken to shore in lifeboats. CBS also mentions that Iran warned ships not to use unapproved routes through the Strait of Hormuz, a detail not included in other accounts.

Sources Associated Press · The Daily Caller · NPR · Axios · BBC · CBS News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Trump’s ex-labor secretary drank on job and created ‘toxic’ work environment, report alleges

Lori Chavez-DeRemer, former U.S. Secretary of Labor under Donald Trump, is accused of creating a "toxic, intimidating and humiliating" work environment, according to a report by the Department of Labor’s Office of Inspector General (OIG). The 38-page report, released by the OIG, details allegations that Chavez-DeRemer drank during working hours, kept alcohol on federal property, and directed employees to perform personal tasks for her. The report also claims she engaged in an inappropriate relationship with a member of her security detail and failed to report gifts properly. The investigation, which began in January 2026, was prompted by an anonymous complaint and involved testimony from 38 witnesses. Chavez-DeRemer resigned in April 2026 amid the allegations.

The report alleges that Chavez-DeRemer used agency funds for personal travel, including at least thirteen trips to family or personal residences and five trips to Las Vegas. It also states that she exceeded allowed reimbursement rates, including three nights at a "luxury hotel and spa" in Palm Beach, Florida. During a personal trip to Oregon, she allegedly requested an off-the-record stop at a club with partially nude dancers and instructed her driver to give money to a performer. The report claims she pressured the driver to comply against his wishes.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and The Daily Wire both mention that Chavez-DeRemer directed employees to organize her bedroom closet during work hours, while ABC News and The Daily Caller do not specify the nature of the task. The Guardian and The Daily Wire describe the incident in detail, including the requirement to provide a video documenting the work. The Daily Caller and The Daily Wire mention that Chavez-DeRemer gave a shoulder massage to the ASAIC during a car ride, which is not included in The Guardian or ABC News. The Guardian and The Daily Wire report that Wright evaluated applicants based on appearance and weight, while The Daily Caller and The Daily Wire also mention that Wright discouraged an employee from using the DOL daycare center due to the race of the caregivers. The Guardian and The Daily Wire include specific details about Wright’s alleged comments about an employee’s hair length, which are not mentioned in The Daily Caller or ABC News.

Sources The Guardian · NPR · ABC News · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Ceiling collapses inside Kennedy Center amid strong storm

A section of the ceiling inside the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts collapsed during severe storms on Friday evening. The incident occurred in the Grand Foyer, a main hallway connecting the center’s three primary performance spaces. Photos showed a large hole in the ceiling and debris scattered across the red carpet. No one was injured, according to Kennedy Center officials. The main building was closed Friday night, while the Grand Foyer is expected to remain restricted through the weekend as crews assess and repair the damage.

Kennedy Center officials, including Vice President of Public Relations Roma Daravi, stated the incident highlights the urgent need for renovations, which are supported by President Donald Trump and the center’s board. The collapse is attributed to decades of deferred maintenance, according to Daravi, who emphasized the necessity of closing the building for renovations.

Where the accounts differ

Just The News and The Guardian both report the collapse occurred in the Grand Foyer and that no one was injured. The Washington Examiner adds that the ceiling fell in the main building and that the area where the ceiling collapsed was the same place where Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-OH) posed for pictures on Wednesday. The Guardian and FOX News mention that the incident may be used by the Trump-aligned board to push for a two-year closure. The Washington Examiner and The Guardian note that a federal judge blocked the board’s initial attempt to close the center for two years, while FOX News states the board voted in August to close the building for two years. The Guardian and FOX News also mention the proposed renaming of the center with Trump’s name, which is contested in court. The Washington Examiner and The Guardian report that the Department of Justice has threatened to demolish the center if the renovations are not approved, while FOX News states that the board remains in court fighting to move forward with the name changes, closure, and renovations.

Sources Just The News · Washington Examiner · The Guardian · FOX News

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

U.S. ambassador calls ongoing West Bank settler violence an "act of terror"

U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee condemned Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank again on Saturday, calling the behavior an "act of terror" during a visit to the village of Turmus Ayya. Huckabee described attacks such as burning cars, torching mosques, and vandalizing homes as criminal acts that extend beyond crime into terrorism. He emphasized that the U.S. Embassy cannot investigate criminal activity but can pressure the Israeli government to address these issues. Huckabee met with about 10 Palestinian American residents who described the impact of the violence on their lives and properties. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the actions of a "handful of rioters" last week, while Israel’s Foreign Ministry described the settlers’ conduct as "a disgrace." According to the United Nations, settler attacks against Palestinians exceeded 1,800 incidents in 2025. More than 1,000 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank since October 2023, according to Palestinian health authorities, a figure that includes those killed by Israeli settlers, while dozens of Israelis have also been killed.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner mentions that Huckabee clarified his remarks were directed toward U.S. citizens living among Palestinians in the region, while CBS News states Huckabee made clear he was addressing U.S. citizens who make up a small percentage of the roughly 3 million Palestinians in the West Bank. The Daily Caller reports that Huckabee put the number of violent settlers at “a few hundred who are responsible, but that’s a few hundred too many.” The Washington Examiner and CBS News do not specify a number, while The Daily Caller provides a numerical estimate. The Washington Examiner also notes that Huckabee emphasized the U.S. Embassy does not have the authority to investigate criminal activity, but CBS News and The Daily Caller do not mention this clarification. The Washington Examiner and CBS News both cite the United Nations stating settler attacks exceeded 1,800 incidents in 2025, while The Daily Caller cites the United Nations humanitarian office for the same statistic.

Sources Washington Examiner · CBS News · The Daily Caller

No source labeled left covered this story.

Judge lets Pentagon move forward with firing Stars and Stripes journalists

A federal judge allowed the Pentagon to proceed with firing three employees of the Stars and Stripes military newspaper. The judge ruled that the government likely did not violate their First Amendment rights by terminating publisher Max Lederer, editor-in-chief Erik Slavin, and reporter Lara Korte. The firings occurred after the newspaper published an article about deteriorating conditions on the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier. The journalists were placed on administrative leave and later fired over allegations of insubordination. The judge noted that the journalists' interviews with CBS News for a "CBS Sunday Morning" segment were part of their official duties, and thus their speech was not protected under the First Amendment.

The lawsuit argued that the Pentagon unlawfully terminated the journalists for speaking out about the need for editorial independence. The judge, however, found that the journalists were acting within their official roles when they gave interviews to CBS News. The ruling came after a court hearing where attorneys for the journalists claimed the interviews were conducted as sources, not as reporters, and were on matters of public concern. The judge dismissed these claims, stating that the journalists' speech was part of their job duties and thus not protected.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News states that the journalists were given separation notices in August and placed on administrative leave, while The Guardian mentions that Lederer declined to present them and opted to resign, but was fired before he could do so. CBS News reports that the interviews with CBS News were for a "CBS Sunday Morning" piece that aired in July, while The Guardian does not specify the timing of the interviews. CBS News includes an email from Korte expressing concern about government control, which The Guardian does not mention. The Guardian notes that McFadden is a Donald Trump appointee, which CBS News does not state.

Sources CBS News · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

Far-right AfD predicted to win big in crucial German state election

The Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), a far-right, anti-immigration party, is expected to win a significant victory in the regional election in Saxony-Anhalt. Polls indicate the AfD is leading with around 40-41% of the vote, ahead of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) at 23% and the Social Democratic Party (SPD) at 8.5%. The AfD's top candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, has predicted gaining an absolute majority, which would allow the party to form a government without needing to cooperate with mainstream parties. The election is seen as a potential turning point for the AfD, which could mark the first time a far-right party holds state-level power in Germany since World War II.

The AfD's platform includes policies such as a "remigration and deportation offensive," a ban on LGBTQ rainbow flags at public schools, and an end to new windfarms. The party has also tapped into nostalgia for communist East Germany and resentment over economic disparities with the west. The prospect of an AfD-led government has raised concerns among mainstream parties and minority groups, with some fearing the party's pro-Russia stance could lead to leaks of sensitive information to Moscow. The German Economic Institute warned that the AfD's immigration policies could be "ruinous" for the state, which has an aging and shrinking population reliant on foreign-born workers.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and Al Jazeera both report that the AfD is predicted to win with 40-41% of the vote, while CBS News and BBC mention similar figures. NPR provides more detail on Ulrich Siegmund's personal brand and his social media presence, including his TikTok following and his carefully curated appearance. The Guardian and BBC note that the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt branch is classified as "right-wing extremist" by Germany's domestic intelligence agency, while CBS News and Al Jazeera also mention this classification. The BBC and CBS News report that the AfD's platform includes a "remigration and deportation offensive," while the Guardian and Al Jazeera also mention this. The Guardian and BBC mention the AfD's pro-Russia stance and fears of leaking information to Russia, while CBS News and Al Jazeera also note this concern. The Guardian and BBC report that the AfD's candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, has been dubbed "Germany's most dangerous man" by Der Spiegel, while CBS News and Al Jazeera also mention this.

Sources The Guardian · NPR · CBS News · BBC · Al Jazeera

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.
